meta_description: What CBT is, what it aims to do, how we work, what research says and what to bear in mind.
title: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy
lead: CBT is based on the idea that our thoughts, feelings and behaviour influence one another.

sections.title: What it is
sections.body:
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is a structured form of psychotherapy with strong research support.

When certain thoughts or habits become unhelpful, they can keep anxiety, sadness and other difficulties going. In therapy we explore these cycles together and try practical ways to change them.

sections.title: What it aims to do
sections.body:
- Identify thoughts and beliefs that make life harder and look at them more realistically.
- Develop practical skills for managing emotions and stress.
- Gradually approach situations we avoid because of fear or anxiety.
- Set specific goals and track progress together.
- Give you tools you can keep using after therapy ends.

sections.title: How we work
sections.body:
1. Initial assessment: understanding what troubles you and what you would like to change.
2. Agreeing on goals and a plan together.
3. Structured sessions with a clear focus and practical exercises.
4. Exercises between sessions, so new skills are tried in everyday life.
5. Regular review of progress and, towards the end, relapse prevention.

sections.title: What research says
sections.body:
Research reviews show that CBT has particularly strong support for anxiety disorders and good support for depression, in adults as well as in adolescents. Outcomes vary from person to person.

Sources: [Hofmann et al. (2012)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3584580/), [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/)

sections.title: Compared with other approaches
sections.body:
There is no single “best” psychotherapy for everyone. Studies comparing the main approaches often find similar outcomes. CBT's strengths are its structure, its focus on specific goals, its practical skills and, often, a shorter duration.

Other approaches may suit people who want to explore their personal history in depth. We can talk about this at our first meeting.

sections.title: Who it is for
sections.body: Adults, couples and adolescents (with age-appropriate techniques and, where needed, parental involvement). Typical topics: anxiety, panic attacks, social anxiety, phobias, depression, stress, sleep problems, low self-esteem. Sometimes collaboration with a psychiatrist is needed.

sections.title: What to bear in mind
sections.body: CBT asks for active participation and practice between sessions. When gradually facing fears or difficult thoughts, it is normal to feel temporary discomfort. Progress varies, and nobody can guarantee a specific outcome.

cta_title: Would you like to talk about it?
cta_text: At our first meeting we will see together whether CBT fits what you are going through.
